newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian killings turn spotlight on shadowy groups.
newsitem.headline: Algerian killings turn spotlight on shadowy groups.

text.p: The killing of 38 people reported in Algeria at the weekend has again turned the spotlight on the shadowy groups blamed by Algerian authorities for many of the deaths in the North African country's five years of violence.
Thirty-one of the dead were victims of a feud between Moslem rebel groups, according to a source close to security forces.
The usually well-informed Algerian newspaper El Watan said Moslem "terrorists" killed them in an Algerian town and a dwarf hacked off their heads with an axe and knife.

Security officials reported on Sunday that seven more people were "assassinated in a cowardly way" -- the usual term for having their throats cut -- the previous night. But, unusually, the officials did not accuse Moslem fundamentalists.

The deaths brought to more than 230 the number reported killed during the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan, which began on January 10. Days earlier the Armed Islamic Group (GIA), the most ruthless of the Algerian fundamentalist groups, issued a warning that it would step up attacks during the month.

The U.S. State Department and the human rights group Amnesty International have said that security forces carry out some of the killings in Algeria, but two groups dominate the conflict in which about 60,000 people have died.
The GIA's mainly young supporters use knives, guns and bombs against civilians and security forces alike, sparing neither babies nor the old.
The group is led by Antar Zouabri, who said in a statement last month: "There is no neutrality in the war we lead. Except for those who are with us, all the others are renegade."

The group claims responsibility for massacres in isolated communities and bombings in the capital Algiers. Four of the five men who hijacked an Air France plane on Christmas Eve 1994 and were killed in Marseille were GIA members, authorities say.

It has also condemned foreigners to die if they stay in Algeria. In a newspaper interview, one unnamed GIA leader called foreigners "the main coronary artery" of a plan to "colonise" Algeria with non-Moslems. "Killing and fighting them is the practical message to weaken the unbeliever rulers," he said.
A key qualification for leaders is that "they should experience armed operations and must demonstrate that they have killed significant numbers among God's enemies", he said.

Six GIA leaders have been killed since December 1992 when it issued "communique number one". Two more were captured and condemned to death, including Mansouri Meliani, executed by firing squad in 1993.
Rivalling the GIA is the Islamic Salvation Army (AIS), which rapidly established itself early in the conflict and is the armed wing of the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS).

Most AIS men are young, fervent and impelled by the belief that they have little to lose in battling authorities. They drew their inspiration from FIS hardliners, who opposed the party's taking part in the December 1991 general election.
When the now outlawed FIS took a commanding lead and the authorities scrapped the poll, the hardliners saw this as evidence that power would come only through force.

But the AIS and the FIS have distanced themselves from the indiscriminate killing of civilians. The AIS, in a statement last week saying it had killed a dozen security force members, said it was not responsible for bombings or civilian deaths.
A lesser-known group, the Algerian Jihad Islamic Front (FIDA), last week claimed responsibility for killing UGTA union leader Abdelhak Benhamouda, one of the best-known victims.

The FIDA is believed to be the armed wing of the elitist Moslem fundamentalist group known as al Djazaraa, which seeks to root Islam in Algeria's secular culture. In a statement, it announced that more Algerian "personalities" would be killed.
A former GIA leader, Djamel Zitouni, killed last July, ordered the elimination of FIDA members and leaders after an aborted unity bid between the two factions in 1994.
Mohamed Said and Abderrazak Redjam, former leading figures in the FIS, were killed in 1995 along with more than 15 FIDA members at the hands of GIA guerrillas.
The FIDA was dealt a heavy blow last year when the security forces killed nine FIDA activists in a two-day standoff in Algiers. Its leader Mohamed Ibrahimi was killed shortly after.

Another Islamist group of which little is known, calling itself The Faithful of the Sermon, said in a recent "communique number one" that Algeria's future would be "more bloody and the earth will tremble under the feet of the tyrannical regime".
